AnyMatchUtility.summary: Every `jdkList.stream().anyMatch(...)` call leaves 6 to 7 objects (160 to 176 bytes) behind for the garbage collector. `Iterate.anySatisfy` and `Iterate.anySatisfyWith` on the same `java.util.List` leave none: 0 bytes per call at every match position, 0 GC runs. At 10 million calls per second the stream version alone allocates about 1.6 to 1.8 GB/s, which is the heap headroom an application has to keep in reserve for a traffic spike; the EC versions need none. EC is also several times faster here (see the table), but the memory difference is the point: it is constant per call, so it grows linearly with load.
AnyMatchUtility.garbage:
*Pipeline garbage (JDK only, measured).* Each `stream().anyMatch()` call builds a `ReferencePipeline$Head` (48 B), an `AbstractList$RandomAccessSpliterator` (32 B), a `MatchOps$MatchOp` (24 B), a `MatchOps$1MatchSink` (24 B) and a `MatchOps` lambda (16 B). These are pipeline plumbing and exist no matter what lambda you pass.

*Lambda garbage (measured).* On top of that the JDK call allocates the captured method reference `Integer.valueOf(this.test)::equals` (16 B) and, for `test = 500` and `1000`, the `Integer` box (16 B; values outside -128..127 are not cached). Escape analysis cannot remove them because they escape into the pipeline objects. In the EC calls the same capturing lambda never escapes `Iterate.anySatisfy`, so escape analysis removes it and the histogram shows nothing.
AnyMatchUtility.ea: With escape analysis off, the lambda shape becomes visible. `ecAnySatisfy` (capturing) allocates 16 B at `test = 1` (the lambda) and 32 B at `test = 500/1000` (lambda plus `Integer` box). `ecAnySatisfyWith` (fat-free) allocates 0 B at `test = 1` and 16 B at `test = 500/1000`: only the `Integer` box from autoboxing `this.test`, an `int`, into the `Object` parameter. So the fat-free form halves the garbage, and removes it entirely when the parameter is already an object. The JDK stream allocates the same 160 to 176 B with or without escape analysis: its garbage does not depend on the JIT at all.
AnyMatchUtility.spike: The derived numbers above use the measured bytes per call. They assume every call allocates the same amount, which the histograms confirm (exactly 1.00 of each object per call).
AnyMatchUtility.coh:
Compact headers shrink the JDK stream's garbage from 176 to 160 B (test = 1) and 192 to 176 B (test = 500, and in the histogram at 1000), about 9%. Object counts do not change. Only objects whose size crosses an 8-byte boundary get smaller (`ReferencePipeline$Head` 56 to 48 B, the `MatchOps` lambda 24 to 16 B). The best fix is still to not allocate: compact headers save 16 B per call, the fat-free EC call saves all 160 to 176 B.

Unexpected, measured: on this machine the EC loops ran about 15 to 20% *faster* with compact headers off (for example `ecAnySatisfy` at `test = 1000`). *Inferred:* `Integer.equals` checks the class of every element, and with compact headers the class pointer has to be decoded from the header word. Check this on the Mac before quoting it.
AnyMatchUtility.supporting:
*Fixed vs per-element cost.* EC: about 2.3 ns at `test = 1` and about 0.65 ns per element scanned (`test = 1000`). JDK: about 30 ns fixed cost to build and tear down the pipeline, plus about 3.0 ns per element at `test = 1000`, so the JDK is slower per element too, not only at setup.

*Rerun.* The first `coh-on` run of this class overlapped with a short chart-rendering test on the same machine, so it was rerun on its own after the full run; the analysis uses the rerun. The overlapped files are kept as `AnyMatchUtility-coh-on.overlapped.*`.

CountUtility.summary: Every `stream().filter().count()` call leaves 7 to 8 objects (208 to 224 bytes) behind. `Iterate.count` and `Iterate.countWith` on the same `java.util.List` leave none, and trigger no GC. Count always scans all 1000 elements, so the cost per call is flat across `test`. At 10 million calls per second the stream version needs about 2.1 to 2.2 GB/s of young-generation space; the EC versions need none.
CountUtility.garbage:
*Pipeline garbage (JDK only, measured).* `ReferencePipeline$2` for `filter` (56 B), `ReferencePipeline$Head` (48 B), `AbstractList$RandomAccessSpliterator` (32 B), `ReduceOps$CountingSink$OfRef` (24 B), `ReferencePipeline$2$1` (16 B) and `ReduceOps$5` (16 B).

*Lambda garbage (measured).* The captured method reference (16 B) and, for `test = 500/1000`, the `Integer` box (16 B). They escape into the pipeline, so escape analysis cannot remove them. In the EC calls the same lambda does not escape and is removed.
CountUtility.ea: With escape analysis off: `ecCount` (capturing) allocates 16 B at `test = 1` and 32 B at `test = 500/1000` (lambda plus box). `ecCountWith` (fat-free) allocates 0 B at `test = 1` and 16 B at `test = 500/1000`, only the `Integer` box from autoboxing `this.test`. The JDK stream allocates the same 208 to 224 B either way.
CountUtility.coh:
Compact headers take the JDK garbage from 224 to 208 B (test = 1) and 240 to 224 B (test = 500/1000), about 7%, with the same object count. `ReferencePipeline$Head` (56 to 48 B) and `ReferencePipeline$2$1` (24 to 16 B) shrink.

Unexpected, measured: the EC loops ran 12 to 18% faster (at `test = 500/1000`) with compact headers off on this machine. *Inferred:* class-pointer decoding in `Integer.equals`. Check on the Mac.
CountUtility.supporting:
*Fixed vs per-element cost.* Both scan all 1000 elements every time. EC: about 0.65 ns per element. JDK: about 1.3 µs per call, roughly twice the EC time.

*Earlier run.* The earlier run showed very wide error bars on `jdkCount` at `test = 1` and `500` (±35%). This run does not: ±6%. The earlier spread was most likely noise on that machine, not a property of the code.

FindFirstUtility.summary: Every `stream().filter().findFirst().orElse(0)` call leaves 7 to 8 objects (200 to 216 bytes) behind. All four EC variants on the same `java.util.List` (`detectOptional`, `detectWithOptional`, `detectIfNone`, `detectWithIfNone`) leave none and trigger no GC, including the two that return an `Optional`: escape analysis removes it because the caller unwraps it straight away. At 10 million calls per second the stream version needs about 2 GB/s of young-generation space.
FindFirstUtility.garbage:
*Pipeline garbage (JDK only, measured).* `ReferencePipeline$2` (56 B), `ReferencePipeline$Head` (48 B), `AbstractList$RandomAccessSpliterator` (32 B), `ReferencePipeline$2$1` (16 B), `FindOps$FindSink$OfRef` (16 B) and the `Optional` (16 B).

*Lambda garbage (measured).* The captured method reference (16 B) and, for `test = 500/1000`, the `Integer` box (16 B).

*The `Optional`.* Both `findFirst` and `detectOptional` must return an `Optional`. In the JDK it escapes through the pipeline and is always allocated. In EC it is created and unwrapped in the same inlined call, so escape analysis removes it (measured: 0 B with escape analysis on, 16 B with it off).
FindFirstUtility.ea: With escape analysis off: `ecDetectIfNone` (capturing) 16 B / 32 B (lambda, plus box at 500/1000); `ecDetectWithIfNone` (fat-free) 0 B / 16 B (box only); `ecDetectOptional` (capturing) 32 B / 48 B (lambda + `Optional`, plus box); `ecDetectWithOptional` (fat-free) 16 B / 32 B (`Optional`, plus box). So the fat-free versions always save exactly the 16-byte lambda, and the `*IfNone` versions also avoid the `Optional`. The JDK stream allocates 200 to 216 B either way.
FindFirstUtility.coh:
Compact headers take the JDK garbage from 224 to 200 B (test = 1, histogram) and 240 to 216 B (test = 500/1000), about 10%. `ReferencePipeline$Head`, `ReferencePipeline$2$1` and `FindOps$FindSink$OfRef` each shrink by 8 B.

Unexpected, measured: EC loops were 12 to 20% faster (at `test = 500/1000`) with compact headers off on this machine. *Inferred:* class-pointer decoding in `Integer.equals`. Check on the Mac.
FindFirstUtility.supporting: *Fixed vs per-element cost.* EC: about 2.4 ns at `test = 1`, about 0.65 ns per element. JDK: about 37 ns fixed cost, about 3.3 ns per element at `test = 1000`.

AnyMatchEagerLazy.summary: On an EC `ImmutableList`, `anySatisfy`, `anySatisfyWith` and `asLazy().anySatisfy` all leave 0 bytes per call and trigger no GC. The JDK `stream().anyMatch()` on a `java.util.List` leaves 6 to 7 objects (160 to 176 B) per call. With escape analysis off, the `ImmutableList` `anySatisfyWith` is *not* fat-free in EC 13.0.0: it allocates the same as the capturing version (see below), which is worth raising with the EC project.
AnyMatchEagerLazy.garbage:
*JDK (measured).* Same 6 to 7 objects as in `AnyMatchUtility`: `ReferencePipeline$Head`, `RandomAccessSpliterator`, `MatchOps$MatchOp`, `MatchOps$1MatchSink`, a `MatchOps` lambda, the captured lambda, and the `Integer` box at `test = 500/1000`.

*EC (measured).* Nothing at or above 0.5 objects per call for any variant, eager or lazy.
AnyMatchEagerLazy.ea: With escape analysis off: `ecAnySatisfy` 16 B / 32 B, `ecLazyAnySatisfy` 32 B / 48 B (adds the `LazyIterable` adapter), and `ecAnySatisfyWith` **16 B / 32 B, the same as the capturing version**. Reason (checked in the EC 13.0.0 bytecode): `ImmutableArrayList` inherits `anySatisfyWith` from `AbstractRichIterable`, which calls `Predicates.bind(predicate, parameter)` and allocates a bound predicate on every call. The `Iterate.anySatisfyWith` utility used in `AnyMatchUtility` loops directly and does not. Only `detectWithOptional` is overridden in `ImmutableArrayList`.
AnyMatchEagerLazy.coh:
JDK garbage: 160 to 176 B (test = 1) and 176 to 192 B (500/1000) without compact headers, about 9% saved. EC: nothing to save.

Unexpected, measured: EC loops 13 to 20% faster (at `test = 500/1000`) with compact headers off. *Inferred:* class-pointer decoding in `Integer.equals`. `jdkAnyMatch` at `test = 500` with compact headers off took 3,918 ns against about 1,585 ns elsewhere; its error is ±3,208 ns, so treat that single cell as noise.
AnyMatchEagerLazy.supporting: *Eager vs lazy.* With escape analysis on, `asLazy()` adds no measurable time and no garbage. With it off, it adds one 16 B adapter per call.

CountEagerLazy.summary: On an EC `ImmutableList`, `count`, `countWith` and `asLazy().count` all leave 0 bytes per call and trigger no GC. The JDK `stream().filter().count()` leaves 7 to 8 objects (208 to 224 B) per call. Count scans all 1000 elements, so time per call is flat; EC is about twice as fast.
CountEagerLazy.garbage:
*JDK (measured).* Same 7 to 8 objects as in `CountUtility`: `ReferencePipeline$2`, `ReferencePipeline$Head`, `RandomAccessSpliterator`, `ReduceOps$CountingSink$OfRef`, `ReferencePipeline$2$1`, `ReduceOps$5`, the captured lambda, and the box at 500/1000.

*EC (measured).* Nothing at or above 0.5 objects per call.
CountEagerLazy.ea: With escape analysis off: `ecCount` 16 B / 32 B, `ecLazyCount` 48 B / 64 B, and `ecCountWith` **16 B / 32 B, the same as the capturing version**: `ImmutableArrayList.countWith` is inherited from `AbstractRichIterable` and allocates a `Predicates.bind` wrapper per call (EC 13.0.0 bytecode). `Iterate.countWith` (see `CountUtility`) does not.
CountEagerLazy.coh: JDK garbage: 208 B vs 224 B (test = 1) and 224 B vs 240 B (500/1000) with and without compact headers, about 7% saved. EC: nothing to save. EC loops were 8 to 21% faster with compact headers off (*inferred:* class-pointer decoding).
CountEagerLazy.supporting: *Eager vs lazy.* No difference with escape analysis on. With it off, `asLazy().count` allocates 32 B more than eager `count`.

FindFirstEagerLazy.summary: On an EC `ImmutableList`, all six EC variants (`detectOptional`, `detectWithOptional`, `detectIfNone`, `detectWithIfNone`, and the lazy `detectOptional` / `detectIfNone`) leave 0 bytes per call and trigger no GC. The JDK `stream().filter().findFirst()` leaves 7 to 8 objects (192 to 216 B) per call.
FindFirstEagerLazy.garbage:
*JDK (measured).* Same objects as in `FindFirstUtility`, including the `Optional` that escapes through the pipeline.

*EC (measured).* Nothing at or above 0.5 objects per call; the `Optional` returned by `detectOptional` is removed by escape analysis.
FindFirstEagerLazy.ea: With escape analysis off: `ecDetectIfNone` 16 B / 32 B; `ecDetectWithIfNone` **16 B / 32 B, the same as the capturing version** (inherited from `AbstractRichIterable`, allocates a `Predicates.bind` wrapper); `ecDetectOptional` 32 B / 48 B; `ecDetectWithOptional` 16 B / 32 B (overridden in `ImmutableArrayList`, so only the `Optional` plus the box); `ecLazyDetectIfNone` 32 B / 48 B; `ecLazyDetectOptional` 48 B / 64 B. So on an `ImmutableList` only `detectWithOptional` is genuinely fat-free in EC 13.0.0.
FindFirstEagerLazy.coh: JDK garbage: 192 to 200 B vs 224 B (test = 1) and 216 B vs 232 to 240 B (500/1000), about 10% saved. EC: nothing to save. EC loops were 14 to 25% faster (at `test = 500/1000`) with compact headers off (*inferred:* class-pointer decoding).
FindFirstEagerLazy.supporting: *Eager vs lazy.* No difference with escape analysis on. With it off, each lazy variant adds one 16 B adapter.
